newsitem.title: PERU: Aeroperu ends search for Boeing crash victims.
newsitem.headline: Aeroperu ends search for Boeing crash victims.

text.p: Peruvian airline Aeroperu said on Friday it has called off its five-week search in the Pacific Ocean for victims of the Boeing, 757-200 crash that killed all 70 people on board.

"Aeroperu has adopted the decision to conclude the work of search and recovery, basing this exclusively on the recommendation of experts," a company statement said. The operation ended late on Thursday.

The bodies of just 52 of the 61 passengers and nine crew members have been recovered from the sea, 50 miles (80 km) northwest of the coastal capital Lima, where the Boeing went down on Oct. 2, airline officials said.

The decision to end the search angered some of the relatives of the victims waiting in Peru. "For humanity's sake we plead with the Peruvian authorities and Aeroperu officials to finish the rescue of our relatives," said the weeping mother of one of 30 Chilean passengers killed.
"They are only asking for two or three days more to finish the rescue," said Antonio Paya, spokesman for the Chilean familes.

Aeroperu, however, insisted it had done everything possible to find all the bodies. Some were floating on the surface but most were with the main wreckage more than 475 feet (200 meters) under water. "Aeroperu has not spared any financial, technical or personnel efforts," the statement said.

Debate raged in Peru over the cause of the accident after the government's controversial announcement this week that adhesive tape covering height and speed sensors on the plane may have caused the tragedy.

Boeing and Aeroperu officials insisted it was "premature" to name a cause. The Peruvian airline pilots' association first alleged "sabotage" in the placing of the tapes prior to takeoff, then changed its version to blame Lima air traffic control for failing to guide the pilot properly.
U.S. aviation authorities studying the "black box" flight recorders in Washington have so far reserved judgment.

The Peruvian government had previously blamed technical faults that made computers aboard the plane "go crazy," leaving pilot Eric Schreiber without instruments as he struggled to return to Lima in the middle of the night.
"We've lost the basic instruments, both for height and for speed ... Where am I? Over land or sea?" he said during a dramatic, 29-minute dialogue with Lima air traffic control.

In addition to the Chileans, the victims included 20 Peruvians, six Mexicans, four U.S. citizens, two Italians, two Britons, two Ecuadoreans, a New Zealander, a Spaniard, a Venezuelan and a Colombian.
